content_voiceover: This page reviews three overlapping topics, gene therapy, inhibitor bypassing strategies, and factor thirteen deficiency. On hemophilia gene therapy, the correct concept is that it uses adeno-associated virus, or AAV, as a vector to deliver a functional gene into liver cells so the body can manufacture its own factor, and it was hemophilia A where this approach first achieved clinical success. A crucial caveat is pre-existing immunity, if a patient has previously been exposed to a particular AAV serotype, neutralizing antibodies can cause a future gene therapy attempt with that same vector to fail, so vector history matters. Emicizumab's dosing schedule can extend out to once every three weeks in some regimens, and it improves long term joint outcomes and quality of life through steady prophylactic cofactor mimicry. Liver transplant is not the standard recommendation despite curing hemophilia in theory, because it's far too invasive relative to modern factor and non-factor therapies. For a severe hemophilia A patient who has developed a factor eight inhibitor, the appropriate treatment arsenal includes recombinant factor seven a, activated prothrombin complex concentrate, emicizumab as the bispecific antibody, and extended half life factor concentrates, essentially all of the modern bypassing and non-factor options. Finally, on factor thirteen deficiency, remember that bleeding tends to be delayed rather than immediate, can include intracranial hemorrhage and poor wound healing, neonates classically present with umbilical stump bleeding, and routine screening tests like bleeding time and thrombin time are typically normal since factor thirteen acts after clot formation to stabilize the fibrin mesh. Severe factor thirteen deficiency is managed with monthly, not weekly, prophylactic dosing of plasma derived factor thirteen concentrate, reflecting its unusually long half life of about nine to fourteen days, and cryoprecipitate does contain factor thirteen and can be used to stop bleeding.
keypoints: AAV-based gene therapy targets liver cells; prior exposure to the same AAV serotype can cause treatment failure
All major bypassing/non-factor options apply to inhibitor patients: rFVIIa, APCC, emicizumab, extended half-life factor
Liver transplant is not standard hemophilia treatment despite being curative in theory
Factor XIII deficiency causes delayed bleeding with normal bleeding time and thrombin time
Severe FXIII deficiency prophylaxis is monthly dosing, reflecting its long 9-14 day half-life
keypoint_voiceover: Three things to hold onto. Gene therapy uses AAV vectors into liver cells, and prior exposure to that same viral vector can sabotage a later treatment attempt. For inhibitor patients, the full modern toolkit includes recombinant factor seven a, A P C C, emicizumab, and extended half life factor, while liver transplant is not standard practice. And for factor thirteen deficiency, expect delayed bleeding with a normal bleeding time and thrombin time, classic umbilical stump bleeding in neonates, and prophylaxis dosed monthly rather than weekly because of its long nine to fourteen day half life.
